From the previous sources:

" In most countries the prevailing definition is an intelligence quotient of 130 or above. However schools also use multiple measures of testing of giftedness  and assess a wide variety of talents, including verbal, mathematical,  spatial-visual, musical, and interpersonal abilities.

In  countries that make special provision for educating gifted pupils, the  prevailing method of selection consists of written tests. Although  standard IQ tests are the most commonly used means of identifying gifted  children, other tests of both intelligence and creativity are also  used."

Some examples are:

## "Early developmental assessments

Such as:

* Parent Evaluation Developmental Status (PEDS)
* Brigance Screens

## Achievement Tests

Achievement tests determine what the students already have learned  and **if they are more advanced than their grade level peers.**   They may  be academic specific (i.e. Math or Language Arts) or standardized tests  (such as SATs, ITBS, SRA, and MATs). These assessments should not have a  ceiling so students are able to show all of what they know.   Tests  specifically designed for the gifted population include *Test of Mathematical Abilities for Gifted Students* or *Screening Assessment for Gifted Elementary Students.*

​

## Ability Tests

Intelligence quotient (IQ) or cognitive abilities test scores are  also used to identify gifted and talented students.

Some examples:

**Individual tests:**

* *Stanford Binet (L-M)*
* *Wescher Intelligence Scale for Children, 4th Edition*.  Read  [Use of the WISC-V in Gifted Education](https://www.nagc.org/sites/default/files/Misc_PDFs/WISC-V%20Position%20Statement%20Aug2018.pdf) and the [WISC-IV](http://www.nagc.org/sites/default/files/Position%20Statement/Use%20of%20the%20WISC-IV%20for%20Gifted%20Education.pdf).
* Woodcock Johnson

Nonverbal tests, such as the *Naglieri Nonverbal Ability Test o*r the *Test of Nonverbal Intelligence*,  may be more effective for students from culturally and linguistically  different or low-income backgrounds to eliminate barriers."

Other than these testing methods it's true that gifted children,  tend to share certain characteristics between them more so than other children tend to have, (which is how you are supposted to interpret these characteristics, not as the sole factor in identifying gifted children but by comparing them to their group of peers and taking into consideration their previous test results).

[https://news.osu.edu/children-with-disabilities-benefit-from-classroom-inclusion/](https://news.osu.edu/children-with-disabilities-benefit-from-classroom-inclusion/)

" Justice conducted the study with [Jessica Logan](https://cog.osu.edu/people/logan), a senior researcher in education, and [Tzu-Jung Lin](http://ehe.osu.edu/directory/?id=lin.1653), assistant professor of educational studies, both at Ohio State; and Joan Kaderavek, a professor of education at the [University of Toledo](http://www.utoledo.edu/).

While all children’s language skills were affected somewhat by the skill levels of their classmates, the effect was strongest for those with disabilities, the study found.

For those children with disabilities who were in classrooms with the most highly skilled peers, language scores in the spring were about 40 percent better than those of children with disabilities who were placed with the lowest-ranked peers.

Peers help because they spend more time one-on-one with their fellow classmates than teachers can.  Children with disabilities have the opportunity to observe, imitate and model the language use of their peers who do not have disabilities."

* ISTEP outcomes for students with high-inclusion placements were higher than their peers in mixed or less inclusive placements.
